text: You have an n by n grid of elevations. At time t, every cell with elevation at most t is underwater and swimmable. Return the least time to swim from the top-left to the bottom-right.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — at time t I can stand on any cell with height at most t, and I move between adjacent flooded cells. Right? Here's the thing I want to say early. To finish a given path, the water only has to be as high as the tallest cell on that path. So the answer is the path whose maximum cell is smallest — a minimax, or bottleneck, path. It's not about the sum of heights. Are heights a permutation of zero to n squared minus one?
Yes, distinct values zero to n squared minus one.

Let me use a small grid: zero, two, one; five, eight, three; six, seven, four. The low path zero, two, one, three, four reaches the corner, and its tallest cell is four. The wall of five, six, seven, eight is never needed. So the answer is four.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to DFS every path and take the min of the max. That's exponential. This problem reminds me of a minimax bottleneck path, and that pattern has three standard tools. I'll show all three: a Kruskal-style rising waterline with union-find, a Dijkstra that relaxes with max instead of plus, and binary search on the answer, because reachability is monotonic in t.

Here's the plan for the primary one — the rising waterline. Here, I'm using union-find to keep track of which flooded cells are connected. One: flood cells in increasing height, like Kruskal adds edges. Two: after flooding a cell, union it with its already-flooded neighbors. Three: the moment start and end share a component, that height is the answer. One thing worth flagging. Because I add cells from lowest to highest, the first height that connects start to end is exactly the smallest water level that works — there's no path using only strictly smaller cells, or they'd already be connected. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Good. Code it, and show me the other two.

Alright, let me code this up, the union-find waterline first. One thing worth flagging is the connectivity check right after each flood: start and end having the same root. The heights come out of the min-heap in increasing order, so the first time this passes, h is the minimum level that links the corners. Now the same minimax two other ways. Dijkstra, but I relax with max, not plus: a neighbor's cost is the max of my cost and its height. And binary search on the answer, since a bigger t only ever floods more cells; a BFS checks reachability. Across the three: union-find relies on adding cells in sorted order, Dijkstra on max being monotonic so the greedy pop is safe, and binary search on reachability being monotonic in t. Same minimax fact, three angles.

Let's dry-run the waterline on that grid — expected four. I flood cells in height order and union with flooded neighbors. Heights zero to three build up the start, the top row, and the cell above the corner into one component. The row that matters is height four: flooding the corner links it to that already-connected low path, so start and end share a component and I return four. Heights five through eight are never flooded. That matches. Corner cases: a one-by-one grid returns its only height. And the answer is always at least the max of the start and end heights, since you must stand on both — that's exactly the binary-search lower bound.

Let me think about complexity here. All three are n squared log n. Union-find and Dijkstra pay the log for the heap over n squared cells; binary search does log of n squared rounds of an n squared BFS. The space complexity is n squared, for the parent array, the dist grid, or the seen grid. In the worst-case scenario the whole grid is one giant blob, but each of the three still stays within that bound. Oh, one more thing — if I had to pick one, I'd take Dijkstra: it only explores cells reachable from the start and stops the instant it pops the corner, whereas the union-find version pushes all n squared cells into the heap up front and floods every low cell, connected or not.

Nice. Three things stood out. You reframed it as a minimax bottleneck path — the tallest cell, not the sum. You gave three standard tools and named exactly what each relies on — sorted insertion, max-relaxation, and monotonic reachability. And you tied the lower bound, the max of start and end, to the binary-search range. Strong hire.
